note_claims.claim: The presenting complaint is fever and right earache.
The fever started on Monday evening and lasted three days, with a maximum temperature of 38.9 °C at home.
The patient has been pulling at the right ear and was unsettled overnight.
The patient has reduced appetite but is drinking well, consuming juice and milk.
The patient has had one episode of vomiting on Tuesday and no subsequent vomiting or diarrhoea.
The patient has had a runny nose for about a week preceding the current symptoms.
The patient has had chickenpox two weeks prior.
The patient is alert and playing this morning.
The patient has no breathing difficulty.
The patient's immunisations are up to date.
The patient has been given paracetamol intermittently.
The patient has no regular medications and no known drug allergies.
The patient's vital signs are Temperature 38.4 °C, Heart Rate 130, and Respiratory Rate 26.
The patient's hands and feet are warm, and the capillary refill is under two seconds.
The left tympanic membrane is normal, and the right eardrum is red and bulging.
The patient's throat is mildly erythematous, and the chest is clear with no rash.
The impression is Right acute otitis media with no features of serious bacterial illness.
The patient has recent chickenpox contact.
The plan includes regular analgesia with paracetamol 180 mg (7.5 mL of 250 mg/5 mL) up to four times daily and ibuprofen 100 mg (5 mL of 100 mg/5 mL) three times daily with food.
A back-up prescription for amoxicillin 250 mg three times daily for 5 days is planned, to be collected only if the patient does not improve after three days or if symptoms worsen.
A leaflet on chickenpox information is given.
Urgent care (999 or A&E) is required if the patient develops a non-blanching rash, becomes very drowsy or hard to rouse, struggles to breathe, or stops drinking and not passing urine.
Contact GP or 111 if the fever lasts more than five days in total, if there is ear discharge, or if the patient does not improve after three days.
The patient should be reported if chickenpox develops and the patient seems very unwell.

transcript_facts.fact: The patient has had a temperature and keeps pulling at her ear.
The duration of the fever was corrected from two days to three days, starting Monday evening (the night of her swimming lesson).
The temperature measured last night was 38.9 °C.
The patient has been pulling at the right ear, mostly.
The patient reports that her ear hurts.
The patient is not eating much but is drinking okay (juice and milk).
The patient is in pants during the day but is still weeing normally, a few times today already.
The patient was sick once on Tuesday but has not since, and has no diarrhoea.
The patient has had a runny nose for about a week before all this started.
The patient has no rash, and her brother had chickenpox two weeks ago.
The patient has never had chickenpox.
The patient is grumpy but herself and was playing with her brother this morning.
The patient reports no problems breathing.
The patient is healthy and all her vaccinations are done.
The patient has no regular medicines and no known drug allergies.
The patient has been given Calpol only when she seems really bad.
Examination findings include Temperature 38.4 °C, Heart Rate 130, Breathing Rate 26, warm hands and feet, and capillary refill under two seconds.
The patient states that her rabbit's ears are fine.
Examination findings include the left eardrum being normal, the right eardrum being red and bulging, and the throat being a little red.
Examination findings include no rash on her skin.
The clinician suggests the finding looks like a middle ear infection on the right side, which usually gets better on its own within three days.
The clinician suggests giving paracetamol 180 milligrams (7.5 mL of 250 mg/5 mL) up to four times a day for pain.
The clinician suggests giving ibuprofen 100 milligrams (5 mL of 100 mg/5 mL) three times a day with food for pain.
A back-up prescription for amoxicillin 250 milligrams three times a day for 5 days is planned, to be collected only if the patient does not improve after three days or if she is getting worse.

Safety netting advice includes calling 999 or going straight to A&E if the patient gets a non-blanching rash, becomes very drowsy or hard to wake, struggles to breathe, or stops drinking and not passing urine.
Safety netting advice includes contacting the GP or 111 if the fever lasts more than five days in total, if there is ear discharge, or if the patient does not improve after three days.
The clinician advises that chickenpox may develop in the next week or so since she has been exposed, and to let them know if she seems very unwell with it.
